html:
The Yukaghir are a small people of northeastern Siberia, shown on the map in 1530 and 1600 in the lowlands of the Kolyma and Indigirka rivers near the Arctic coast. They call themselves Odul.

They lived by hunting wild reindeer and elk and fishing the rivers, and some groups herded reindeer. Their languages are not related to those of their neighbours and are counted among the Paleo-Siberian tongues. Before the Russians came they seem to have held a much wider range, from the Lena east toward the Anadyr, next to the Chukchi. The Turkic-speaking Yakuts and the Tungusic Evens pressed on them from the south and west.

Cossacks reached their rivers in the 1630s and 1640s during the Russian conquest of Siberia and forced them to pay tribute in furs. War and smallpox cut their numbers sharply, and many merged with their neighbours. Today about 1,600 people count themselves Yukaghir, and their two languages have few speakers.
